newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil bent on re-election despite vote scandal.
newsitem.headline: Brazil bent on re-election despite vote scandal.

text.p: The Brazilian government is determined to push on with a Senate vote Wednesday on President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election bid, despite continuing fall-out from a money-for-votes scandal, officials said.

"We vote tomorrow. Our impression is that the furor over the vote-buying scandal won't interfere because it's a matter for the Chamber of Deputies and not the Senate," said an aide to Senator Jose Roberto Arruda, the government leader in Congress.

The government and financial markets were rocked last week by reports in the Folha de Sao Paulo newspaper that five deputies from the state of Acre allegedly accepted $190,000 in bribes for voting in favor of the re-election bill.
Cardoso had denied any wrongdoing, as have the five congressmen reportedly involved in the scheme.
Communications Minister Sergio Motta, allegedly named in a taped conversation between a deputy implicated in the scam and a mysterious "Mr X", has angrily denied any involvement.

Officials admit the scandal has dented the government's image. But Cardoso's popularity was already on the wane before the news broke, according to a poll published Tuesday in the Estado de Sao Paulo newspaper.
The survey showed Cardoso's approval rating had fallen to 50 percent just before the Folha report from 70 percent in March.

The re-election bill, passed by the Chamber in January and facing the first of two votes in the Senate Wednesday, allows presidents, governors and mayors to seek a second consecutive term for the first time since the republic was founded in 1889.
Political analysts said they expected the government to win the ballot but felt the bill would be changed to make sitting governors stand down six months before seeking re-election.
Senators considering running in the next gubernatorial polls fear that if governors stayed in office, they might use the political machinery of their state to gain an unfair advantage.

Analysts and government officials in Congress said the reported involvement of governors Amazonino Mendes of Amazonas and Orleir Cameli of Acre in the vote-buying scam -- which the governors have denied -- made it more likely senators would vote to force governors to step down.
"The government has already conceded that point," said an official, asking not to be identified.

"The government needs the support of governors to have re-election passed. But everyone is aware that this is perhaps the political price that must be paid. It's the only way," said political analyst Ricardo Pedreira of Santafe Ideias.
An internal congressional investigation into the Folha revelations was due to report Tuesday but its members requested an additional 24 hours to complete their probe.

The investigators had been hoping to quiz former federal deputy Narciso Mendes, suspected by some journalists and politicians of being "Mr X". But Mendes declined to attend a hearing, saying he had nothing to say that would "enrich" the probe's final report. His wife, currently deputy Celia, Monday said that as far as she knew her husband was not involved with the recording of any tape linked to the scandal.
Opposition parties have been campaigning for a full-blown Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry (CPI), which the government fears would stall all work in Congress.
A spokesman for the leftist Workers Party said 211 deputies had so far signed up to a CPI. The motion needs 257 signatures if it is to be given priority and leap to the front of the CPI waiting list.
"We're pretty confident we'll get them," the spokesman said.
